title: Golden Eagle breeding response to utility-scale solar development and prolonged drought in California
abstract: Each year from 2012–2016, we conducted helicopter surveys to monitor the distribution, success, and productivity of Golden Eagles (Aquila chrysaetos) breeding within 16 km of California Valley Solar Ranch (CVSR) in San Luis Obispo County, California. This 250-megawatt photovoltaic solar plant was built over 2 yr on 642 ha of disturbed grassland and desert scrub habitat on Carrizo Plain, and was operational in October 2013. Beginning in 2012 coincident with initial CVSR development, the study area and region experienced a severe drought that persisted through the end of the 2016 breeding season. During the study, we detected and monitored 19 variably occupied Golden Eagle breeding territories. We confirmed a similar number of occupied territories in 2012 (15) and 2016 (16), but our ability to reliably confirm pairs declined during the drought and shifting territory dynamics occurred in several areas. Between 2012 and 2015, the proportion of pairs that laid eggs (breeding rate) and fledgling production per occupied territory (productivity) declined by 93–95% (13 pairs laid eggs in 2012; only 1 pair did so in 2015). In 2016, the breeding rate increased sharply again to 63% of occupied territories (87% in 2012) following the return of average rainfall during the preceding winter, but the proportion of pairs that fledged young and productivity rebounded to notably lesser degrees. The eagle breeding rate and productivity trends were strongly correlated with current-year measures of primary plant productivity and rainfall totals from the previous water-year (June–July). Breeding performance metrics for five pairs with territories situated on the periphery of Carrizo Plain and 13 pairs located elsewhere in the study area away from possible development disturbance did not differ statistically. This suggested that CVSR development and initial operation did not adversely affect eagle breeding performance during the study; however, we cannot draw definitive conclusions from this 5-yr study about how CVSR development might have influenced the local eagle breeding population. Instead, we concluded that a severe 5-yr drought dramatically reduced eagle breeding activity in the study area (and region) and confounded our effort to evaluate the effects of the solar development.

## Golden Eagle Breeding Response to Utility-Scale Solar Development and Prolonged Drought in California

**Article** _in_ Journal of Raptor Research · May 2020 DOI: 10.3356/0892-1016-54.2.154

California Energy Commission View project

## GOLDEN EAGLE BREEDING RESPONSE TO UTILITY-SCALE SOLAR DEVELOPMENT AND PROLONGED DROUGHT IN CALIFORNIA

JEFF P. SMITH,[1] COLLEEN M. LENIHAN, AND JEFFREY A. ZIRPOLI[2] H. T. Harvey & Associates, 983 University Avenue, Building D, Los Gatos, CA 95023 USA

ABSTRACT.—Each year from 2012–2016, we conducted helicopter surveys to monitor the distribution, success, and productivity of Golden Eagles (Aquila chrysaetos) breeding within 16 km of California Valley Solar Ranch (CVSR) in San Luis Obispo County, California. This 250-megawatt photovoltaic solar plant was built over 2 yr on 642 ha of disturbed grassland and desert scrub habitat on Carrizo Plain, and was operational in October 2013. Beginning in 2012 coincident with initial CVSR development, the study area and region experienced a severe drought that persisted through the end of the 2016 breeding season. During the study, we detected and monitored 19 variably occupied Golden Eagle breeding territories. We confirmed a similar number of occupied territories in 2012 (15) and 2016 (16), but our ability to reliably confirm pairs declined during the drought and shifting territory dynamics occurred in several areas. Between 2012 and 2015, the proportion of pairs that laid eggs (breeding rate) and fledgling production per occupied territory (productivity) declined by 93–95% (13 pairs laid eggs in 2012; only 1 pair did so in 2015). In 2016, the breeding rate increased sharply again to 63% of occupied territories (87% in 2012) following the return of average rainfall during the preceding winter, but the proportion of pairs that fledged young and productivity rebounded to notably lesser degrees. The eagle breeding rate and productivity trends were strongly correlated with current-year measures of primary plant productivity and rainfall totals from the previous water-year (June–July). Breeding performance metrics for five pairs with territories situated on the periphery of Carrizo Plain and 13 pairs located elsewhere in the study area away from possible development disturbance did not differ statistically. This suggested that CVSR development and initial operation did not adversely affect eagle breeding performance during the study; however, we cannot draw definitive conclusions from this 5-yr study about how CVSR development might have influenced the local eagle breeding population. Instead, we concluded that a severe 5-yr drought dramatically reduced eagle breeding activity in the study area (and region) and confounded our effort to evaluate the effects of the solar development.

KEY WORDS: Golden Eagle; Aquila chrysaetos; breeding ecology; drought; helicopter surveys; population response; solar development.

Esta planta solar fotovoltaica de 250 megavatios fue construida durante 2 a ̃nos en 642 ha de ha ́bitat de pastizales antropizados y matorrales dese ́rticos en la Llanura de Carrizo, y comenzo ́ a operar en octubre del 2013. Desde principios del 2012, coincidente con el comienzo del desarrollo del RSVC, el a ́rea de estudio y la regio ́n experimentaron una sequ ́ıa severa que persistio ́ hasta fines de la estacio ́n reproductiva del 2016. ## [Traduccio ́n del equipo editorial]

California Valley Solar Ranch (CVSR) is a 250megawatt (MW), utility-scale, photovoltaic solar power plant located on Carrizo Plain in eastern San Luis Obispo County, California, USA (Fig. 1). The facility was built in an area of primarily disturbed, annual grassland just north of Carrizo Plain National Monument. The National Audubon Society (2019) designated Carrizo Plain a California Important Bird Area, reflecting the importance of the extensive grassland and shrubland habitat for wintering raptors and other birds.

The Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act (US Fish and Wildlife Service 2009, 2016) prohibits actions in the United States that compromise the survival and productivity of Golden Eagles (Aquila chrysaetos). Relevant actions include those that cause direct mortality as well as those that indirectly reduce eagle productivity and survival, such as modifying foraging habitat to a degree sufficient to cause abandonment of breeding territories, reduced breeding success and productivity, or lower survival of adults or juveniles. Golden Eagles do not nest on Carrizo Plain itself, because the grassland landscape generally lacks suitable nest substrates and favorable topography. They do commonly nest in the adjacent hills and ranges, however, are known to forage throughout the year on Carrizo Plain, and were observed on the CVSR site prior to development (Latta 2010, H. T. Harvey & Associates 2011). Reflecting concerns that the development might adversely affect the foraging ecology and productivity of breeding eagles, the Avian and Bat Protection Plan developed for the project (per requirements of conditional use permit DRC2008-00097 issued by the San Luis Obispo County Board of Supervisors) stipulated annual monitoring of the local Golden Eagle breeding population commencing with the

onset of construction and continuing for 3 yr postconstruction (H. T. Harvey & Associates 2011).

To help describe a local population of breeding Golden Eagles that may be affected by a development project, the US Fish and Wildlife Service (2009, 2016) recommends conducting surveys within a 16-km radius of the proposed development footprint. CVSR construction began in late 2011 and the facility was considered operational in October 2013. We conducted annual, helicopter-based monitoring of breeding Golden Eagles within a 16-km radius of the CVSR site during the 2012–2016 breeding seasons (late February/early March through early June). The goal of the study was to help determine whether CVSR development influenced the breeding activities of Golden Eagles whose home ranges potentially overlapped the site. Because the study unexpectedly coincided with a major drought cycle, it also provided an opportunity to evaluate how the Golden Eagle breeding population responded to that climatological event.

## METHODS

Study Area. The Carrizo Plain is a closed-drainage subbasin situated in the southeastern Coast Ranges of California at an average elevation of 594 masl. The enclosed plain is bounded by the Temblor Range on the east (highest elevation 1320 masl) and the Caliente and La Panza Ranges on the west (highest elevation in La Panza Range 1176 masl; Fig. 1), with the Central Valley located east of the Temblor Range. CVSR is located in the east-central Carrizo Plain with a project footprint that encompasses approximately 642 ha) of facility infrastructure comingled with 1324 ha of designated conservation lands, with another 2347 ha of off-site conservation areas designated as part of the project’s mitigation requirements (H. T. Harvey & Associates 2011,

Figure 1. Study area (16-km-radius primary survey area outlined in black) around California Valley Solar Ranch on Carrizo Plain in eastern San Luis Obispo County, California, USA.

2017). Soda Lake, a 1505-ha alkaline lake, is located 4.8 km south in Carrizo Plain National Monument. Otherwise, the surrounding area comprises privately owned land that is sparsely developed, occasionally farmed, and mostly open rangeland.

Open grassy hillsides and shrublands predominate on the western flanks of the Temblor Range, with natural eagle nest substrates generally limited to isolated Fremont cottonwoods (Populus fremontii) and blue oaks (Quercus douglasii) in limited areas. In

comparison, the east side of the Temblor Range provides many more potential natural eagle nest substrates in the form of comparatively extensive blue and valley oak (Q. lobata) woodlands, cliffs, and rocky outcrops. Much of the La Panza Range features even more extensive blue and valley oak woodlands and savannas, as well as relatively mesic riparian corridors, but also some boulder-strewn and chaparral-dominated ridges adjacent to Carrizo Plain. The Caliente Range, situated to the south in

Carrizo Plain National Monument, is drier and supports more juniper (Juniperus spp.) and desert scrub along ridges, but also broad expanses of grazed grassland and oak savanna with isolated cottonwoods in drainages. In addition to the potential natural nest substrates found in the area, several high-voltage transmission power lines traverse the Temblor Range and Carrizo Plain and support many Golden Eagle, Red-tailed Hawk (Buteo jamaicensis), and Common Raven (Corvus corax) nests. Eagles that forage on the Carrizo Plain include both area residents and seasonal visitors, but the relative prevalence of different population segments is unknown, as are the ranging dynamics of eagles that breed in the area.

Our study area encompassed 1279 km[2] within a 16-km radius of the CVSR project footprint, including roughly 41 linear km of the Temblor Range (east and west sides) and portions of the montane habitats and associated drainages along the western margins of Carrizo Plain (Fig. 1). In a few areas, our monitoring extended up to 1.3 km outside of the 16km-radius primary survey area to encompass all known alternative nests for relevant breeding pairs. Latta (2010) surveyed a similar area by helicopter in 2010, but extended his survey farther west and north to encompass a 16-km radius of CVSR and the 500 MW Topaz Solar Farm (11 km northwest of CVSR; visible in Fig.1). Both facilities were proposed at that time and ultimately were developed in a similar timeframe.

Terminology Used to Describe Breeding Activity. Terminology and metrics used to describe and quantify territory occupancy and breeding performance (Appendix) generally follow McIntyre and Schmidt (2012), Steenhof and Newton (2007), and Steenhof et al. (2017). We estimated only apparent breeding success (Steenhof and Newton 2007) rather than employing modeling techniques to account for incomplete coverage of possible early breeding failures (Shaffer 2004). Our approach might have overestimated the probability of success if we missed any early failures; however, a relatively early start to the surveys minimized that bias.

Survey Methods. We conducted aerial surveys from a Bell Jet Ranger Model B206BII helicopter following guidelines outlined in Pagel et al. (2010) and employing two individuals each with more than 15 yr of experience conducting Golden Eagle nest surveys. Each year, we typically conducted three rounds of aerial surveys, with the goal of achieving a comprehensive inventory of occupied Golden Eagle

breeding territories and obtaining estimates of breeding success and productivity for all known pairs. The first round of surveys in late February or early March documented territory occupancy, nest tending, and egg laying. The second round of aerial surveys in mid-April confirmed late nest initiations and hatching. The third round of aerial surveys in late May or early June confirmed breeding success and fledgling production. In a few cases, we conducted follow-up ground surveys to confirm the final status of selected and accessible late nests, and in 2015 we did not conduct a third aerial survey because we had only one ground-accessible nest to check. Survey rounds often included multiple visits to individual territories to secure necessary information. We conducted all surveys during fair weather with good visibility and, at most, moderate winds.

We used a GPS-enabled iPadt equipped with GIS Prot software (Garafa, LLC, Provo, UT, USA) to facilitate navigation and record data, survey tracks, and coordinates for all nests. We documented initial nest coordinates while hovering 100–200 m above the nest location, and later verified their accuracy using Google Eartht. We used a Canon 60D digital camera equipped with an image-stabilized 100–400 mm lens to further document nest locations, structures, and contents. We used the photographic guides provided in Hoechlin (1976) and Driscoll (2010) to age nestlings, and we used photographs to confirm or adjust our initial field estimates of activity status and nestling ages.

Metrics of Landscape Condition. To characterize the annual landscape condition in the study area, we used residual dry matter (RDM) metrics from a concurrent, annual monitoring study of the CVSR conservation lands (H. T. Harvey & Associates 2017); annual water-year (July–June) precipitation totals recorded approximately 6.4 km west of CVSR (San Luis Obispo County Public Works 2016); and regional drought maps produced by the National Drought Mitigation Center (2019). RDM is a standard used by land management agencies to assess plant growth and the influence of livestock grazing (George et al. 1996, Bartolome et al. 2006) and, as a measure usually recorded in fall, is indicative of the preceding season’s plant production. RDM typically is assessed using a class scale that reflects the estimated kg/ha of herbaceous vegetative matter, with higher class values representing lower RDM and diminished vegetative growth during the recent growing season. The class scale used during the CVSR RDM assessments to evaluate

39–63 sample plots per year was: 1 1⁄4 .3375 kg/ha, 2 1⁄4 2363–3375 kg/ha, 3 1⁄4 1125–2363 kg/ha, 4 1⁄4 563– 1125 kg/ha, 5 1⁄4 338–563 kg/ha, and 6 1⁄4 ,338 kg/ ha.

To estimate area-wide RDM means on a nonordinal scale where higher values indicated higher primary productivity, we replaced each year- and plot-specific class code with the midpoint value of the relevant RDM measurement range (estimated for class 1 to be the minimum plus an increment proportional to preceding class differences). Annual means calculated across all sampled plots then formed the basis for evaluating correlations with annual Golden Eagle breeding rate and productivity metrics. The translated data also supported a simple ANOVA with Tukey post-hoc comparisons to discern significant (P ,0.05) interannual differences in primary productivity, as measured by RDM assessments. We developed all statistical analyses using Systat 13.2 (Systat Software, Inc., San Jose, CA, USA)

Golden Eagle Breeding Rates and Productivity. We evaluated interannual variation in breeding performance metrics from 2012–2016. We used Pearson v[2] tests to discern differences in annual proportions of occupied territories, breeding attempts, and breeding successes. We used ANOVAs with Tukey post-hoc comparisons to discern differences in annual productivity estimates. We calculated Pearson correlations to evaluate relationships between annual Golden Eagle breeding rates and productivity estimates and annual RDM and precipitation indices. Because Golden Eagle breeding responses often lag a year or more behind causal changes in landscape conditions and prey populations (Bates and Moretti 1994, Kochert et al. 1999), we also calculated correlations with annual rainfall totals lagged 1 yr (e.g., 2010–2011 water-year rainfall correlated with 2012 breeding rate and productivity estimates). An absence of 2011 RDM data precluded a similar lagged analysis.

To help evaluate whether CVSR development influenced the breeding performance of Golden Eagles in the study area, we compared the breeding rate, breeding success, and productivity estimated for two groups defined based on whether the pairs’ breeding-season home ranges were or were not likely to overlap Carrizo Plain. The first group comprised pairs with breeding territories located around the periphery of Carrizo Plain, in the western Temblor Range and eastern La Panza and Caliente Ranges. The second group comprised pairs with breeding territories located elsewhere in the study area, in the

eastern Temblor Range, central and southern La Panza Range, and central Caliente Range (see Supplemental Materials for additional location details). We used pooled variance t-tests to compare breeding performance metrics for the two groups.

## RESULTS

Climatic and Landscape Conditions. As defined by the National Drought Mitigation Center (2019), the study area was not experiencing abnormally dry conditions in January 2012, but moderate drought conditions were evident by January 2013, extreme drought conditions by January 2014, and exceptional drought conditions by the end of 2014. Exceptional drought conditions then persisted across the region through the end of the 2016 breeding season, despite the return of limited rainfall during winter 2014–2015 and normal rainfall during winter 2015– 2016. Annual rainfall totals were above average in 2010 and 2011, declined steadily to 34% of average by 2014, increased again to 73% of average in 2015, and increased again to 104% of the 48-yr average in 2016 (Fig. 2).

The marked decline in precipitation during the 2012–2014 water years contributed to a loss of plant productivity on the Carrizo Plain and in surrounding areas (H. T. Harvey & Associates 2017). The median RDM class value on the CVSR conservation lands was 4 in 2012, increased to 5 in 2013 (representing a 40– 50% decline in average herbaceous cover), increased to 6 in 2014 (representing a further 33% decline in average herbaceous cover), dropped back to 5 in 2015, and stayed at that level in 2016. The ANOVA and post-hoc comparisons confirmed that the decline in primary productivity between 2012 and 2014 was significant (R[2] 1⁄4 0.39, F4, 224 1⁄4 35.4, P ,0.001) and that RDM levels remained below the 2012 (P ,0.001) and 2013 (P 1⁄40.062) levels in 2016 (Fig. 2). The return of moderate precipitation in early 2015 bolstered productivity some and reduced the median RDM class again; however, vegetative growth still remained well below levels observed in 2011 and 2012 (H. T. Harvey & Associates 2017). Average precipitation returned in winter 2015/ spring 2016, but the median RDM class remained high, reflecting the residual adverse effects of prolonged drought on soil moisture.

Latta (2010) documented 11 occupied breeding territories and seven breeding attempts in our study area, and found another nest that was obviously built by eagles on an electrical transmission tower in the eastern Temblor Range, but confirmed no eagles in that territory at the time. In 2012, we determined that all 12 of these breeding territories were occupied by adult pairs, found three additional occupied territories, and confirmed 13 breeding attempts (Table 1).

In 2013, we documented 10 breeding attempts among 15 occupied and 2 likely occupied (previously known) breeding territories. We found pairs in three new areas. In the first case, although we could

not be certain of the eagles’ identities without marked birds, we think one adult pair shifted 7 km farther up into the Temblor Range (same distance from the nearest CVSR boundary) after having nested successfully the previous year at a lowerelevation site (not used again by eagles during this study). An adult pair resided in the new area during the rest of the study, but did not complete a nest and initiate a breeding attempt there until 2016. The other two cases appeared to involve adult breeders that were new or at least partially new (mate turnover possible) to the area, because at least one adult occupied all other known territories that year. One of these pairs built and laid eggs in a new nest on a microwave tower in the western Temblor Range, and the second pair built a new nest in the central La Panza Range but did not initiate a breeding attempt during the study.

The occupied territories included a pair of adult eagles that began inhabiting a new area in the east-central Temblor Range in 2014, but did not build a nest until 2015 and did not initiate a breeding attempt until 2016. Multiyear evidence suggested this was a new breeding pair for the study area.

In 2015, we detected pairs of adult eagles in only 9 of 19 known territories and documented only a single breeding attempt among 14 occupied and 3 likely occupied breeding territories. Although no eggs were laid in them this year, we found new nests under construction in two newer (for the study) territories.

In 2016, we confirmed pairs of adult Golden Eagles in 15 of 19 known territories and documented 10 breeding attempts among 16 occupied territories. The latter included the first breeding attempts during the study in two territories that had been occupied by adult pairs for the preceding 2–3 yr. In one known territory we categorized as occupied for summary purposes, we found the pair electrocuted under a distribution power pole (which served the microwave tower on which the nest was built) and a necropsy confirmed the female was preparing to lay eggs. Otherwise, we found no eagles in one known territory for the third consecutive year and in another known territory for the second

consecutive year. We also found no eagles in a third territory where a failed nesting attempt occurred in 2012, only a single adult occupied the territory in 2013, and we observed an eagle on only one other occasion from 2014–2016.

Breeding Rate, Breeding Success, and Productivity. The breeding rate declined by 94% from 2012 to 2015, then increased again in 2016 back up to the same moderately high level observed in 2013 (Table 1, Fig. 2). Breeding success also declined markedly from 73% in 2012 to 6% in 2014 and 2015, but then rebounded only slightly in 2016 to 25%. Productivity and total fledgling production followed a similar pattern, declining by 95–96% from 2012 to 2015, then rebounding in 2016 but only to a moderate degree compared to the breeding rate.

Trends in annual eagle productivity and estimated RDM levels were positively correlated (r 1⁄4 0.94, P 1⁄4 0.020). Annual breeding rates and RDM levels also were moderately correlated (r 1⁄4 0.67); however, this level of correlation was not statistically significant (P 1⁄4 0.21) based on a sample size of only 5 yr. The difference also reflected a stronger rebound in the breeding rate in 2016 than in the RDM and productivity levels (Fig. 2). Correlations between annual breeding metrics and precipitation during the concurrent water year were less substantial (r 1⁄4 0.24–0.40, P 1⁄4 0.51–0.69); however, introducing a 1-

Pairwise t-tests revealed no significant differences (P 0.25) between occupancy and breeding performance metrics for the five periphery and 13 nonperiphery pairs, though small territory sample sizes limited the power of these tests (Table 2). In addition, human-caused factors not related to solar development compromised the breeding performance of two periphery pairs. Utility maintenance removed one pair’s nest from its transmission tower support before the 2014 breeding season, which was the only year this pair did not fledge at least one young. These eagles quickly began building a new nest on the same tower, but did not complete the nest and lay eggs again until 2015 (the only pair to do so that year). The other compromised periphery pair was the one electrocuted in 2016 just as the female was preparing to lay eggs.

## DISCUSSION

The 2012 and 2013 breeding performance estimates for the study area were moderately high compared to estimates from elsewhere in California, Idaho, Wyoming, Utah, and Alaska (Table 3). Breeding performance in the study area then dropped in 2014 toward the low end of ranges from other long-term studies, and dropped further in 2015 to the extreme low end of comparative values. Other data from central California similarly indicated depressed breeding rates and especially reduced

productivity in 2014 and 2015 compared to previous years. Widespread declines in general raptor breeding performance were also reported from southern California during the peak drought period (J. Kidd pers. comm.). With the return of normal rainfall during winter 2015, eagle breeding performance increased again in 2016 to at least a moderate level in both our study area and among a large well-studied population in the northern Diablo Range of California (centered approximately 275 km northnorthwest of CVSR; Wiens at al. 2018).

The above evidence suggests that the severe drop in eagle breeding performance in the study area between 2012 and 2015 was primarily droughtrelated. The drought reduced plant productivity on Carrizo Plain and in the surrounding hills, and probably contributed to a sustained decline in prey availability for breeding eagles. Although the return to normal rainfall in winter 2015/spring 2016 helped replenish the landscape, the residual effects of severe drought limited the recovery of primary productivity in 2016, and the lagged effect of annual rainfall on Golden Eagle breeding performance suggested it would take multiple years to rebuild prey populations enough to support high eagle productivity again.

The probability of detecting Golden Eagle breeding pairs in the northern Diablo Range of California declined markedly as breeding seasons progressed for pairs that did not nest or failed early (Wiens et al. 2018). Accordingly, although we did not evaluate detection probabilities during this study, it is likely that the difficulty we had confirming breeding pairs during the peak drought period primarily reflected the limitations of periodic aerial surveys for confirming occupancy when territory holders temporarily forgo breeding and wander more widely in search of food (Driscoll 2010, Pagel et al. 2010). It often takes several years of failed or forgone reproduction for an established breeding pair to abandon its territory because of increasing disturbance or deleterious landscape changes (Steenhof et al. 2014). Conversely, a local population may temporarily abandon established territories in the face of an initial development disturbance, but then return several years later once that source of disturbance subsides (Smith et al. 2010).

By the end of this 5-yr study, our observations suggested that, on the east side of the Temblor Range, two former breeding territories were no longer regularly occupied by Golden Eagles, but one new territory was occupied higher up and closer to CVSR. On the west side of the Temblor Range, one territory/nest site was abandoned after a single successful breeding attempt, but we believe that pair shifted 7 km higher up in the Temblor Range and eventually built a new nest that was the same distance from CVSR as their previous nest. In addition, two other new breeding territories were occupied during the study with new nests built and used for nesting (one on the Carrizo Plain periphery and one elsewhere in the study area), and a fourth new territory was occupied for several years and a new nest was built but not used for nesting during the study (located away from the Carrizo Plain periph-

ery). In the end, although the composition of some pairs might have changed, the distribution of breeding activity definitely changed, and we were able to confirm only 10–12 breeding pairs in 2014 and 2015 at the height of the drought, ultimately we documented 15 breeding pairs in 2012 and 16 pairs in 2016 (which the aforementioned electrocution event reduced to 15 pairs again). In addition, the shifting territory dynamics did not appear to reflect pairs seeking to nest farther from the solar development. In general, these findings emphasize the dynamic nature of interannual breeding and ranging activity in a long-lived species, where established pairs often do not nest every year and home ranges may vary considerably in response to variable landscape conditions, especially when influenced by forces such as climatic extremes, large-scale fire, and development activity (Steenhof et al. 1997, 2014; Kochert et al. 1999; Haworth et al. 2010; Smith and Slater 2010; Smith et al. 2010; Watson 2010; Watson et al. 2014; Braham et al. 2015).

Evaluation of Potential CVSR Impacts. Adult Golden Eagles may range many kilometers from their nests in search of prey and their breedingseason home ranges often extend across tens of square kilometers (Kochert et al. 2002); however, available data from similar grassland/savanna and shrubsteppe habitats in the western United States suggest that adult eagles most often forage within 1– 3 km of their nest while provisioning young (Marzluff et al. 1997, Hunt 2002, Watson et al. 2014). Given this foraging range, it appeared unlikely that eagles breeding on the east side of the Temblor Range, in the central and southern La Panza Range, and in the central Caliente Range routinely traveled onto Carrizo Plain to provision their nestlings. Routine foraging across the plain during the breeding season was probable only for the five periphery pairs that occupied territories on the western flanks of the Temblor Range and eastern flanks of the Caliente and La Panza Ranges. Accordingly, if development of the solar facilities and the attendant loss of foraging habitat on Carrizo Plain had a negative effect on the local breeding population, we expected that evidence to emerge among the periphery pairs whose foraging home ranges might have overlapped the solar-development areas.

Other survey data suggested that raptors as a group, including Golden Eagles and several other species, occurred less frequently on the CVSR site during construction and through the first year of operation than on neighboring control plots (H. T.

Harvey & Associates 2015). With no ability to set up a more robust before-after-control-impact study, the unpredictable coincidence of the CVSR development timeline and overriding influence of the drought precluded a more informative evaluation to determine whether the solar development(s) influenced the local eagle breeding population under less extreme landscape conditions. Nevertheless, comparative breeding performance metrics suggested that the five periphery pairs fared no better or worse during the study than breeding pairs with home ranges that likely did not overlap Carrizo Plain. Moreover, had two periphery pairs not suffered human-caused losses unrelated to solar development and nested successfully in the relevant years, all breeding metrics for the periphery pairs would have been further elevated. Thus, although we cannot draw definitive conclusions from this 5-yr study about how CVSR development might have influenced the local eagle breeding population, we can be reasonably certain that severe drought dramatically reduced eagle breeding performance in the study area, as well as elsewhere in California, and confounded our effort to evaluate the effects of the solar development.
